question:
A 23-year-old male arrives at the emergency department with right upper quadrant (RUQ) and
epigastric pain. He describes a 6/10 sharp, intermittent pain accompanied by nausea for the past 3
hours, which started after lunch. He mentions having similar episodes previously that resolved
spontaneously. Over-the-counter pain medication provided no relief. He denies fever, chills, headache,
chest pain, shortness of breath, or urinary symptoms. His medications include methotrexate and folic
acid for Crohn disease. His alcohol consumption is 6-8 beers nightly, with increased intake the previous
night. He denies smoking or drug use. Physical examination reveals RUQ and epigastric tenderness
with a positive Murphy sign. Laboratory findings are as follows: Serum: Na+: 136 mEq/L Cl-: 96 mEq/L
K+: 4.1 mEq/L HCO3-: 23 mEq/L Urea nitrogen: 10 mg/dL Glucose: 115 mg/dL Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP): 145 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase (AST, GOT): 65 U/L Alanine
aminotransferase (ALT, GPT): 43 U/L Bilirubin, total: 2.5 mg/dL Bilirubin, direct: 2.1 mg/dL Lipase: 149
U/L Urine: Epithelial cells: 1/hpf Glucose: Negative WBC: 0/hpf RBC: 0/hpf Bacterial: None What is the
most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms? Answer Choices: (A) Malabsorption of bile acids
(B) Hepatocellular carcinoma (C) Autodigestion of the pancreas (D) Primary sclerosing cholangitis (E)
Obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone (F) Alternating strictures and dilation of intra- and
extrahepatic bile ducts (G) Acute alcoholic hepatitis (H) Functional gallbladder disorder (I) Ischemic
hepatitis (J) Portal vein thrombosis
 A. Alternating strictures and dilation of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts
B. Obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone
C. Acute alcoholic hepatitis
D. Ischemic hepatitis
E. Malabsorption of bile acids
F. Functional gallbladder disorder

G. Hepatocellular carcinoma
H. Primary sclerosing cholangitis
I. Portal vein thrombosis
J. Autodigestion of the pancreas
